positive time step of [latex]\Delta t[/latex]. Let [latex]y_n[/latex] represent the numerical solution obtained after [latex]n[/latex] steps. The condition [latex]|y_{n+1}| \leq |y_n|[/latex] is satisfied if and only if [latex]\Delta t[/latex] does not exceed _____. (Answer in integer)

y_{n+1}=y_{n}+h f\left(x_{n}, y_{n}\right)
[/latex] Given: [latex]\frac{d y}{d t}+2 y=0[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \quad \frac{d y}{d t}=-2 y[/latex] and step size, [latex]\mathrm{h}=\Delta \mathrm{t}[/latex] [latex]\therefore \quad y_{n+1}=y_{n}+\Delta t\left(-2 y_{n}\right)[/latex] [latex]\mathrm{y}_{\mathrm{n}+1}=\mathrm{y}_{\mathrm{n}}(1-2 \Delta \mathrm{t})[/latex] [latex]\frac{y_{n+1}}{y_{n}}=1-2 \Delta t \;\;\;...(i)[/latex] Given: [latex]
\left|y_{n+1}\right| \leq\left|y_{n}\right|
[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \quad\left|\frac{y_{n+1}}{y_{n}}\right| \leq 1[/latex] From equation (i) [latex]\therefore \quad|1-2 \Delta t| \leq 1[/latex] Case (i) when [latex](1-2 \Delta t) \gt 0[/latex] : Then, [latex]\quad 1-2 \Delta t \leq 1[/latex] [latex]
\Delta t \geq 0
[/latex] Case (ii) when [latex](1-2 \Delta t) \lt 0[/latex] : then [latex]-(1-2 \Delta t) \leq 1[/latex] [latex]
1-2 \Delta \mathrm{t} \geq-1
[/latex] [latex]
\Delta \mathrm{t} \leq 1
[/latex] [latex]\therefore \quad[/latex] Value of [latex]\Delta t: 0 \leq \Delta t \leq 1[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Solution of differential equation given by forward Euler's method is
[latex] y_{n+1}=y_{n}+h f\left(x_{n}, y_{n}\right) [/latex]
Given: [latex]\frac{d y}{d t}+2 y=0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \frac{d y}{d t}=-2 y[/latex]
and step size, [latex]\mathrm{h}=\Delta \mathrm{t}[/latex]

Then, [latex]\quad 1-2 \Delta t \leq 1[/latex]

then [latex]-(1-2 \Delta t) \leq 1[/latex]

The velocity profile at section B downstream is [latex]u=\left\{\begin{matrix} V_m\frac{y}{\delta }, & 0\leq y\leq \delta \\ V_m,& \delta \leq y\leq H-\delta \\ V_m\frac{H-y}{\delta }, & H-\delta \leq y\leq H \end{matrix}\right.[/latex] The ratio [latex]V_{m}/u_{0}[/latex]
 is
questions.explanation: Applying continuiting equation at sections A and B, mass flow rate at inlet section A = Mass rate at section B. [latex]m_A=m_B[/latex] Hence, per unit width of the channel, we get [latex]\begin{aligned} \rho u_0 H \times 1 &=\rho V_m(H-2\delta )\times 1+2\rho \int_{0}^{\delta }udy \times 1 \\ u_0 H &=V_m(H-2\delta )+2 \int_{0}^{\delta }\frac{V_my}{\delta }dy \\ u_0 H &=V_m(H-2\delta )+2 \frac{V_m}{\delta } \left [ \frac{y^2}{2} \right ]_0 ^\delta \\ u_0 H &= V_m(H-2\delta )+2 \frac{V_m}{\delta } \times \frac{\delta ^2}{2}\\ u_0 H &= V_m(H-2\delta )+ V_m\delta \\ u_0 H&= V_mH-2V_m\delta +V_m\delta \\ u_0 H&= V_mH-V_m\delta \\ u_0 H &=V_m(H-\delta ) \\ \frac{V_m}{u_0}&=\frac{H}{H-\delta }=\frac{1}{1-(\delta /H)} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question:
The S-N curve from a fatigue test for steel is shown. Which one of the options gives
the endurance limit?
questions.explanation:
For some ferrous (iron base) and titanium alloys,
the S-N curve becomes horizontal at higher N
values; or there is a limiting stress level, called the
fatigue limit (also sometimes the endurance limit),
below which fatigue will not occur. This fatigue
limit represents the largest value of fluctuating
stress that will not cause failure for essentially an infinite number of cycles. For many steels, fatigue
limits range between 35% and 60% of the tensile
strength.

questions.explanation:
Soldering is define as a metal joining process
wherein coalescence is produced by heating the
surface to be joint to a suitable temperature and
melting the filler metal which is a fusible alloy called
solder (melting point usually less than [latex] 427^{\circ}C[/latex]
). Principle underlying soldering is that when the
surface to be jointed are cleaned off well from
oxides they can be joined together using molten
solder that may adhere easily with the workpiece. Brazing is also one of the type of welding process

metal piece together by heating the surface and
by using a non-ferrous filler metal having its melting
point above [latex] 427^{\circ}C[/latex] but below the melting point of
metal to be brazed. The molten filler metal is
distributed between the joint surface by the capillary
action which on cooling results in a sound joint.

angular velocity ratio [latex] |\omega _2|/|\omega _1|=1/4[/latex], have their centers 30 mm apart. The

and [latex] m=\frac{D}{T}=\frac{1}{P_{d}} [/latex]

questions.question:
A spherical ball weighing 2 kg is dropped from a height of 4.9 m onto an
immovable rigid block as shown in the figure. If the collision is perfectly elastic,
what is the momentum vector of the ball (in kg m/s) just after impact? Take the acceleration due to gravity to be [latex]g=9.8 m/s^2[/latex]. Options have been
rounded off to one decimal place.
questions.explanation_html:
Let '[latex]\theta[/latex]' be the angle about line of impact through which ball will move often the impact.
Let '[latex]u[/latex]' be the vertical downward velocity of the ball before striking and '[latex]v[/latex]' be the velocity of ball after the impact which make an angle '[latex]\theta[/latex]' with the line of impact. As ball fall freely under the gravity from height [latex]\mathrm{h}=4.9 \mathrm{m}[/latex], hence downward velocity '[latex]\mathrm{u}[/latex]' at the instance of striking the rigid body
[latex]u=\sqrt{2 g h}=\sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 4.9}[/latex]
or, [latex]u=9.8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{sec}[/latex]
for perfectly elastic collision, [latex]e=1[/latex]
As [latex]e=\frac{\text { relative velocity of seperation }}{\text { relative velocity of approach }}=1\;\;...(i)[/latex]
As block is rigid, so block velocity [latex]=0[/latex].
So, along the line of impact,
relative velocity of approach [latex]=u \cos 30^{\circ}-0 =u \cos 30^{\circ}[/latex]
relative velocity of separation along the line of impact [latex]=v \cos \theta-0=v \cos \theta[/latex]
so, by equation (i)
[latex]u \cos 30^{\circ}=v \cos \theta \;\;\;...(ii)[/latex]
In the direction normal to the impact, the component velocity is not affected so,
[latex]u \sin 30^{\circ}=v \sin \theta \;\;\;...(iii)[/latex]
So, by equation (ii) and (iii)
[latex]V=\sqrt{u^{2} \cos ^{2} 30^{\circ}+u^{2} \sin ^{2} 30^{\circ}}[/latex]
or, [latex]V=9.8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{sec}[/latex]
by equation (ii) and (iii)
[latex]\tan \theta=\tan 30^{\circ}, \theta=30^{\circ}[/latex]
So, inclination to the plane for of the section
[latex]=90^{\circ}-30^{\circ}=60^{\circ}[/latex]
So, momentum equation is given by during seperation:

[latex] \vec{P}_{s}=m v \cos 30^{\circ} \hat{i}+m v \cos 30^{\circ} \hat{j} =17 \hat{i}+9.8 \hat{j} [/latex]

questions.question:
The figure shows a wheel rolling without slipping on a horizontal plane with
angular velocity [latex]\omega _1[/latex]. A rigid bar PQ is pinned to the wheel at P while the end Q
slides on the floor. What is the angular velocity [latex]\omega _1[/latex] of the bar PQ?
questions.explanation_html:
As Disc (Link 2) roll without slipping on Link 1 (surface) so their I-centre of rotation lies on point of contact to avoid relative motion in between them. So [latex]\mathrm{I}_{12}[/latex] lies on point of contact.
Link 2 and 3 have instantaneous center of rotation at [latex]\mathrm{I}_{13}[/latex] due to fixed surface of Link 1.

As per point Plies on link 2 and 3 both so, point [latex]P[/latex] has same velocity for Link 2 and 3 both.
As per Kennedy's theorem, if three plane bodies have relative motion among themselves, their I-centre must lie on a straight line. So, [latex]\mathrm{I}_{23}[/latex] must be on line joining [latex]\mathrm{I}_{13}[/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{I}_{12}[/latex] at point P.
By similar [latex]\triangle \mathrm{PI}_{12} \mathrm{~B}[/latex] and [latex]\Delta \mathrm{Pl}_{13} \mathrm{~A}[/latex], we have
[latex] \frac{\mathrm{l}_{12} \mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{l}_{12} \mathrm{~B}}=\frac{\mathrm{Pl_{13 }}}{\mathrm{PA}} [/latex]
or, [latex]\quad \frac{\mathrm{I}_{12} \mathrm{I}_{23}}{2}=\frac{\mathrm{I}_{23} \mathrm{l}_{13}}{8}[/latex]
or, [latex] \mathrm{I}_{12} \mathrm{l}_{13}=0.25 \mathrm{I}_{23} \mathrm{l}_{13} \;\;\;...(i) [/latex]
Velocity of point [latex]P[/latex] is same w.r.t. all instantaneous rotation so,
[latex] \omega_{1} \times I_{12} I_{23}=\omega_{2} \times I_{23} l_{13} [/latex]
By equation (i), we get
[latex] \omega_{2}=0.25 \omega_{1} [/latex]

options.A: For an ideal gas, the enthalpy is independent of pressure.
options.B:
For a real gas going through an adiabatic reversible process, the process equation is given by [latex]PV^\gamma =[/latex] constant, where [latex]P[/latex] is the pressure, [latex]V[/latex] is the volume and [latex]\gamma [/latex] is the ratio of the specific heats
of the gas at constant pressure and constant volume.
options.C:
For an ideal gas undergoing a reversible polytropic process [latex]PV^{1.5} =[/latex] constant, the equation
connecting the pressure, volume and temperature of the gas at any point along the process is [latex]\frac{P}{R}=\frac{mT}{V}[/latex]  where [latex]R[/latex] is the gas constant and  [latex]m[/latex] is the mass of the gas.
options.D:
Any real gas behaves as an ideal gas at sufficiently low pressure or sufficiently high
temperature.

questions.explanation_html:
Ideal gas follow the adiabatic equation [latex]\mathrm{PV}^{\gamma}=\mathrm{C}[/latex] and also follow the gas law [latex]P V=m R T[/latex]
Any real gas at low pressure and high temperature follow gas law, e.g. Air conditioning system.
Real gas follow Van der waal's gas equation for an adiabatic process as
[latex] \left(P+\frac{n^{2} a}{V^{a}}\right)(V-n b)^{\top}=k [/latex]
where
[latex] \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{T}=\frac{\mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{v}}}+1 \\ & \mathrm{k}=\mathrm{nRZ} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Enthalpy of an ideal gas is independent of pressure at constant temperature and the internal energy of an ideal gas is independent of volume at constant temperature.

rake angle of the tool [latex]\alpha =5^{\circ} [/latex], and the shear angle, [latex] \phi [/latex], is known to be [latex]45^{\circ} [/latex]. Applying the ideal orthogonal cutting model, consider two shear planes [latex]PQ[/latex] and [latex]RS[/latex] close
to each other. As they approach the thin shear zone (shown as a thick line in the figure),
plane [latex]RS[/latex] gets sheared with respect to [latex]PQ[/latex] (point [latex]R1[/latex] shears to [latex]R2[/latex], and [latex]S1[/latex] shears to [latex]S2[/latex]). value of shear strain rate (in [latex]s^{-1} [/latex]) that the material undergoes at the shear zone?

Data given [latex] \alpha=5^{\circ} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \phi & =45^{\circ} \\ \Delta H & =25 \mu \mathrm{m} \\ \mathrm{V} & =1 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{sec} \\ \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{s}} & =\frac{\mathrm{V} \cos \alpha}{\cos (\phi-\alpha)}=\frac{1 \times \cos 5^{\circ}}{\cos (45-5)} \\ & =\frac{\cos 5}{\cos 40}=1.3 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{sec} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Shear strain rate [latex]=\frac{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{s}}}{\delta \mathrm{H}}=\frac{1.3}{25 \times 10^{-6}}=5.20 \times 10^{4} \mathrm{s}^{-1}[/latex]

1-2 \Delta \mathrm{t} \geq-1

questions.question:
The velocity field of a certain two-dimensional flow is given by [latex]V(x,y)=k(x\hat{i}-y\hat{j}) [/latex] where [latex]k=2s^{-1}[/latex]. The coordinates [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex] are in meters. Assume gravitational
effects to be negligible. If the density of the fluid is [latex]1000kg/m^3[/latex]
and the pressure at the origin is 100 kPa,
the pressure at the location (2 m, 2 m) is _____________ kPa.
(Answer in integer)
questions.explanation_html:
To find the pressure at location [latex](2 m, 2 m)[/latex] we apply Bernouli's equation

[latex] P_{1}+\frac{1}{2} \rho V_{1}^{2}=P_{2}+\frac{1}{2} P V_{2}^{2} [/latex]

We will apply this equation between two points Origin [latex](0,0)[/latex] and location [latex](2 \mathrm{~m}, 2 \mathrm{~m})[/latex]

At Origin [latex](0,0)[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} & V=k(x \hat{i}-y \hat{j}) \\ & V_{1}=2(0-0)=0 \\ & P_{1}=100 \mathrm{kPa} \end{aligned} [/latex]

At Iocation [latex](2,2)[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} & V=2(2 \hat{i}-2 \hat{j}) \\ & \vec{V}=4 \hat{i}-4 \hat{j} \end{aligned} [/latex]

magnitude of velocity
[latex] \begin{aligned} & V_{2}=\sqrt{4^{2}+4^{2}}=\sqrt{32} \\ & V_{2}=\sqrt{16 \times 2}=4 \sqrt{2} \end{aligned} [/latex]

Applying Bernouli's theorem
[latex]100,000+\frac{1}{2} \times 1000 \times 0=P_{2}+\frac{1}{2} \times 1000 \times 32[/latex]
So [latex]P_{2}+16,000=100,000[/latex]
[latex] P_{2}=100,000-16,000 [/latex]
[latex] P_{2}=84,000 \mathrm{~Pa}=84 \mathrm{kPa} [/latex]

questions.question: Consider a unidirectional fluid flow with the velocity field given by [latex]V(x,y,z,t)=u(x,t)\hat{i}[/latex] where [latex]u(0,t)=1[/latex]. If the spatially homogeneous density field varies with time [latex]t[/latex] as [latex]\rho (t)=1+0.2e^{-t}[/latex] the value of [latex]u(2,1)[/latex] is _______. (Rounded off to two decimal places) Assume all quantities to be dimensionless.

Continuity equation for unsteady flow [latex]\rho \frac{\partial \mathrm{u}}{\partial \mathrm{x}}+\rho \frac{\partial \mathrm{v}}{\partial \mathrm{y}}+\rho \frac{\partial \omega}{\partial \mathrm{z}}+\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial \mathrm{t}}=0[/latex] Here [latex]V(x, y, z, t)=u(x, t) \hat{i}[/latex] So

[latex]
v=0
[/latex] [latex]
\omega=0
[/latex] [latex]
\rho \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial P}{\partial t}=0
[/latex] Given [latex]\rho(t)=1+0.2 e^{-t}[/latex] So, [latex]\left[1+0.2 e^{-t}\right] \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left[1+0.2 e^{-t}\right]=0[/latex] [latex]
\begin{aligned}
&\left(1+0.2 e^{-t}\right) \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}-0.2 e^{-t}=0 \\
&\left(1+0.2 e^{-t}\right) \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=0.2 e^{-t} \\
& \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=\left[\frac{0.2 e^{-t}}{1+0.2 e^{-t}}\right] \\
& u=\left[\frac{0.2 e^{-t}}{1+0.2 e^{-t}}\right] x+C
\end{aligned}
[/latex] Since [latex]
\begin{aligned}
